Preface
This technical report was produced in 2025, prior to the closure of the Strait of
Hormuz in 2026.1, 2
The report grew out of a shared recognition among the European
Union, FAO, and Agrinatura that a fresh approach is needed – since decades of
subsidy programmes, research and investment have achieved only limited suc
cess in improving soil health and fertilizer use in sub-Saharan Africa. It sets out policy options and decisions that need to be made, and is
aimed at policymakers, development practitioners, and researchers working on
sustainable food systems transformation across Africa. The hope is that it will also prove useful to development finance
institutions and others focused on agrifood systems in the region so they can
deliver sustainable improvements in production, food security and nutritional
outcomes. The report aligns with, and was partly shaped by, the 2024 African
Union Nairobi Declaration: Boosting Africa’s Agricultural Productivity with
Healthy Soils – a political commitment that reflects the need to address these
issues at the highest levels. Since the report’s completion, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz has
introduced new and significant risks to global energy, fertilizers, and food
systems, with particular implications for Africa as a region that relies on imports
for much of its energy and fertilizer needs. Supply disruptions resulting from the conflict, affecting oil, gas, and
fertilizer trade, have already triggered substantial price spikes, with significant
implications for the sub-Saharan smallholder farmers at the heart of this
report. 1 For further information on the impacts of recent developments, please refer to the
FAO brief Global agrifood implications of the 2026 conflict in the Middle East, pro
duced by the FAO Chief Economist’s Office, which analyses impacts on energy and fer
tilizer trade and food security. Additional FAO analytical publications address other

Executive summary
Agriculture is a cornerstone of the economy of sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), con
tributing 17.5 percent of the region's gross domestic product (GDP) and employ
ing more than 60 percent of the population. Yet the sector faces complex and
persistent challenges (World Bank, 2025a), and falls short of meeting the food
security needs of the continent. A fifth of the SSA population faces hunger –
the highest percentage globally (FAO et al., 2025) – and land degradation affects
65 percent of the productive land. Productivity remains low, particularly on small
farms where most food is produced. Although total output has increased over
time, this growth has been driven primarily by converting forest and natural land
into farmland, rather than by productivity gains. These dynamics have reduced
soil carbon storage capacity and diminished soil health, compounding longterm threats to food security. They undermine agricultural productivity and trap
smallholder farmers in a vicious cycle of poor yields, limited resources, and
deteriorating soil conditions. Fertilizers are a key factor in breaking this cycle, yet their efficient use
in SSA remains low due to structural, market and agronomic constraints. Average nitrogen fertilizer use stands at 13.3 kg/ha – roughly a fifth of the global
average of 65.4 kg/ha (FAO, 2024a). High and variable fertilizer prices, driven
largely by import dependence, are compounded by distribution challenges,
inadequate infrastructure, high transaction and transportation costs, import
administration costs and limited market competition. Supply-side constraints
alone, however, do not fully explain low fertilizer use. On the demand side, limitations include inadequate information on soil
type, soil quality, farmers’ perceptions of fertilizer quality, inadequate size pack
aging, ineffective agricultural extension, and limited access to financing, as well
as marketing difficulties that contribute to unprofitability. Fertilizer efficiency is
also undermined by poor soil fertility and health, lack of site-specific recommen
dations, and limited adoption of complementary approaches for sustainable
intensification. These challenges, exacerbated by persistently high prevalence
of poverty (estimated to range between 40 percent and 80 percent across
different SSA countries), constrain effective demand for fertilizer. Underinvestment in agricultural research and development, along with weak
regulatory frameworks – especially for promising options such as bio-based
fertilizers3 – continue to narrow the available options. Crucially, for subsistence farmers, low fertilizer use is often a rational
response to risk rather than simply a matter of limited knowledge or weak incen
tives. Investments in soil health may compete directly with immediate food
security needs of the family. Uncertain returns, climate variability, and weak
output markets further increase the cost of failure. Constraints ranging from

mentation interact and reinforce one another, meaning that progress in one area

analysis offers evidence-based insights that go beyond the existing polarized
debates around fertilizers, to explore a range of policy options and actions aimed

at mitigating further soil degradation, rehabilitating degraded land, and optimiz
ing fertilizer use on both healthy and degraded lands. These perspectives aim
to balance long-term soil health and food security needs of smallholder farmers
with their short-term profitability, and the varying needs of soils and crops. The main approaches to fertilizer application and soil health have
evolved from the green revolution focus on high-yielding varieties and chemical
inputs toward more sustainable, systemic approaches linking smallholder farm
ers, biological processes, and mineral fertilizers. This shift recognizes that while
fertilizers are necessary to increase productivity growth, their effectiveness
depends on proper application and soil conditions. In alignment with the 2024
Nairobi Declaration and the African Union’s Fertilizer and Soil Health Action
Plan, integrated soil fertility management (ISFM) has emerged as a way to opti
mize both bio-based and mineral nutrient use, with fertilizers as an entry point
to sustainable intensification. Agroecology and regenerative agriculture have
also gained prominence, highlighting soil health in enhancing agrifood systems
sustainability, and leading to multiple co-benefits including climate resilience,
biodiversity restoration, ecosystem services and food security. For many resource-constrained smallholders, practices such as inter
cropping, crop rotation, and crop–livestock integration are not transitional steps
toward input-intensive systems. They are core producer strategies for managing
soil fertility and production risk – for which their feasibility is constrained by farm
size, with very small plots often pushing farmers toward continuous monocrop
ping that accelerates soil degradation. In the context of the Africa Fertilizer and Soil Health Action Plan:
2024–2034, this report presents four priority policy options to improve soil
health and sustainably boost food production as critical elements for the sus
tainable transformation of agrifood systems in sub-Saharan Africa. The 2025
Kampala CAADP Declaration, which sets out the Comprehensive Africa
Agriculture Development Programme (CAADP) agenda for 2026–2035,
reaffirms Africa’s commitment to invest in restoring and maintaining soil fertility
and health as a cornerstone of sustainable agrifood systems. Viewed together
as part of an integrated soil health and fertilizer policy framework, these priority
policy options consist of: (i) improving soil health and soil fertility; (ii) increasing
the availability of fertilizers; (iii) increasing access to and affordability of quality
fertilizers; and (iv) increasing producers’ production incentives. The options are
assessed against five criteria: technical efficiency, economic, environmental and
social impact, as well as scalability. This report examines options for enhancing
soil health and efficient fertilizer management
among small-scale farmers in SSA. XII

Within the four policy priorities, the report assesses a diverse set of tools and
options for action that stakeholders could consider and tailor to local contexts. Investment in rural infrastructure (roads, storage, information systems) and
fostering market competition can increase availability and lower farm-gate
fertilizer prices. Expanding local fertilizer production, including mineral fertilizer
manufacturing and blending, green hydrogen-based fertilizer, bio-based
fertilizer, can also enhance fertilizer availability. Policymakers can accompany
these efforts with actions to incentivize farmers’ demand for fertilizers and sus
tainable production practices, by addressing a range of constraints that small
holder farmers may face. Because constraints interact and differ systematically
across farm types, instruments must be differentiated accordingly. For subsist
ence farmers, risk-reduction measures – crop insurance, credit access, and in
come buffers – may need to precede or accompany fertilizer promotion. For semicommercial and commercial farmers, improved market access and site-specific
recommendations are likely more binding constraints. The evidence presented in this report thus points clearly away from
one-size-fits-all approaches to assessing and prioritizing diverse tools and
options. This may require governments to radically rethink fertilizer support
programmes, moving away from strategies that treat smallholders as a uniform
group. To avoid continued underperformance of such blanket methods, coun
tries could consider more flexible, nuanced and comprehensive approaches
along the lines of ISFM to meet the needs of farmers and their soils. Critically, the
efficiency of fertilizer application depends highly on the agronomic conditions
of soil health. Appropriate, relevant approaches could include integrating
mineral fertilizers with ISFM and agroecological practices, such as adequate
nutrient cycling, legume and water management infrastructure, crop-livestock
integration, and biofertilizers. An important finding in the report is that investing
in permanent soil health and infrastructure (e.g. production, market and roads)
yields more sustainable long-term benefits than simply subsidizing fertilizers. Thus, in many settings, market integration and risk reduction will need to ac
company or even precede fertilizer promotion if investments in soil health are to
generate durable returns. Transforming Africa's soil health and fertilizer management will re
quire a multi-pronged approach to inform policy and catalyse investments. This
will need sustained political commitment and coordinated investment through
partnerships between farmers, governments, financial institutions, research
centres, agribusinesses, and stakeholders from sectors beyond agriculture. A strong enabling environment – backed by coherent regulation, robust moni
toring systems, and public-private partnerships – would also contribute to more
sustainable agrifood systems in Africa. The diverse policy tools outlined in this report address trade-offs that
will need to be made. Short-term approaches alone cannot adequately feed
growing populations, while long-term policies often encounter political con
straints. Ideally, countries would define their long-term objectives for sustaina
ble agrifood systems and design and implement policies to move towards these
goals. The African Union and regional economic groupings can play a central
role in holding member states accountable to the long-term agrifood system
strategies and budgets this transformation demands. The analytical tools and
policy frameworks to do this already exist – what remains is the institutional will
to apply them at scale. The knowledge basis and the policy toolbox are ready for
this journey. XIII

1.1
AGRIFOOD SYSTEMS AND SOIL HEALTH IN SUB-SAHARAN AFRICA:
CONTEXT AND BACKGROUND
Sub-Saharan Africa continues to face the challenge of food insecurity. An esti
mated 307 million people living in the region experienced food insecurity in
2024, some 20.2 percent of the population – the highest proportion in the world
(FAO et al., 2025). The persistent lack of food security results from a complex
interplay of factors, including high levels of poverty, low agricultural productivity,
uneven structural transformation, poor infrastructure, weak governance, chron
ic conflict, soil degradation, climate change and weather shocks (CFS, 2021a;
Vanlauwe et al., 2023; Giller, 2020). Agriculture continues to be the foundation of Africa's economy and
contributed 17.5 percent of SSA’s GDP in 2024 (World Bank, 2025a), with signif
icantly higher contributions in countries such as Somalia (55.8 percent) and
Niger (47.8 percent) (World Bank, 2025a). More than 60 percent of the region’s
population relies on agriculture for a livelihood, a figure rising to 80 percent
in Somalia and 86 percent in Burundi (World Bank, 2022a). Approximately
70 percent of food production in low- and middle-income countries comes from
farms smaller than 20 hectares (Woodhill, Hasnain and Griffith, 2020). Agricultural productivity-led growth is a driving force in rural and structural
transformation in SSA, though varying in this role within and between countries
(Gollin, 2023). Traditional pathways for agricultural transformation face significant
challenges in SSA, including constraints on agricultural productivity growth,
farm consolidation and movement of labour to other sectors of the economy. These pathways are hindered by rural population growth, land fragmentation,
and vulnerability to climate change, as well as a lack of value addition and offfarm employment opportunities – critical to raise incomes and enhance food
security (Giller and Andersson, 2024). Introduction

Agricultural productivity growth in Africa as a whole – and particularly in SSA –
remains alarmingly low (Fuglie et al., 2019). The continent lags the rest of the
world, with cereal yields doubling from 0.81 tonnes/ha in 1961 to 1.7 tonnes/ha in
2020 – less than half of global cereal yields estimated at 4.18 tonnes/ha in 2020
(see Figure 1). Panel data (2008–2019) from smallholder farmers across six SSA
countries show no significant improvement in crop total factor productivity
(TFP) (Wollburg et al., 2024),4 despite increasing investments in African agricul
ture over the last 20 years. While total agricultural output has increased over
time, this growth is driven primarily by land expansion (see Figure 2) rather than
significant productivity gains (Giller et al., 2021). Further, extensification through
conversion of forest and other natural land into farmland reduces soil capacity
to store carbon, exacerbating land degradation and contributing to greenhouse
gas emissions (Olsson et al., 2019; Ansari et al., 2022). Africa’s low agricultural productivity growth has been attributed to
several challenges, such as limited input use, restricted access to quality seed,
and heavy reliance on rainfed agriculture with insufficient irrigation infrastruc
ture. These constraints are compounded by soil health issues, including nutrient
mining, climate shocks, food price volatility, and insecure and customary land
tenure (Jayne and Sanchez, 2021). Small African economies struggle with limited capacity for technology
adoption and adaptation, while underinvestment in agricultural R&D hinders the
development of farming techniques suited to the continent’s diverse agro-

Soil health is a key determinant of Africa’s agricultural productivity and food
security, shaping both crop yields and nutritional quality (Montgomery et al.,
2022; Montgomery and Biklé, 2021). Poor soil health remains the major biophysical constraint on agricultural production in SSA (Tittonell and Giller, 2013),
and its consequences extend well beyond agronomy. Nutrient-deficient soils
produce nutrient-deficient crops, contributing to micronutrient deficiencies in
human diets – commonly called “hidden hunger”. The World Health Organization
(WHO) estimates this affects more than two billion people globally, with dispro
portionate impact in Africa, where soil and human zinc deficiencies often overlap
(Cakmak, McLaughlin and White, 2017). Practices that prioritize short-term
yields ahead of soil health have deepened the problem (Mayer et al., 2020). Restoring soil health is therefore essential not only for raising agricultural pro
ductivity but for improving nutrition and public health outcomes across the
continent (FAO, 2022a). Despite widespread awareness of the importance of healthy soils,
degradation6 is serious, and accelerating. The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) estimates that one-third of soils globally
are already degraded (FAO, 2021a), which could increase to 90 percent by 2050
(FAO, 2022b). Africa’s situation is more acute still: up to two-thirds of productive
land (65 percent) is currently degraded (Mansourian and Berrahmouni, 2021). Ineffective land management is a primary driver of this degradation. Although smallholder farmers are the principal stewards of Africa’s agricultural
land, their ability to invest in sustainable practices is constrained by limited
resources, insecure land tenure, weak incentives, and ongoing land fragmenta
tion driven by inheritance customs and laws. Small farm sizes and declining soil
health compound one another in what Giller and Andersson call a “double
poverty trap” (Giller and Andersson, 2024) – where poor soils reduce yields and
low yields leave farmers without the means to restore soil health. ISFM offers a pathway forward, combining the judicious use of mineral
fertilizers with bio-based inputs, improved germplasm, and locally adapted
agronomic practices. However, the potential of this approach is held back by the
prevalence of both excessive and insufficient fertilizer application, which contin
ues to impede soil fertility regeneration (Vanlauwe et al., 2023). Attitudes and approaches to soil fertility have evolved considerably,
as summarized in Table 1. Vanlauwe et al. (2023) trace the shifts: from the green
revolution’s emphasis on high-yielding varieties and synthetic fertilizers, to the
emphasis on smallholder systems, biological processes and low-external-input
sustainable agriculture (LEISA) of the 1990s. ISFM subsequently emerged as a
pragmatic approach that emphasized optimizing the combined use of mineral
and bio-based nutrients and of fertilizers as an entry point into the sustainable
intensification of smallholder systems. Concurrently, concerns about soil ero
sion and loss drove major investments in conservation agriculture. More recently,
agroecology and regenerative agriculture have gained attention, both emphasiz
ing soil health as central to productivity growth and ecosystem services. Agroecology and regenerative agriculture are often interpreted as emphasizing
minimal use of fertilizer and other inputs. Vanlauwe et al. (2023) argue that
across all these approaches, environmental, social and human dimensions must
be integrated into efforts to build and sustain soil health. 6 Soil degradation is defined as a change in the soil health status resulting in a di
minished capacity of the ecosystem to provide goods and services for its beneficiar
ies. Degraded soils have a health status such that they do not provide the normal
goods and services of the particular soil in its ecosystem. (See FAO, 2021a).

Political recognition of the importance of soil health and fertility has grown, as
reflected in the Nairobi Declaration of the 2024 Africa Fertilizer and Soil Health
Summit. African leaders affirmed that building soil health and regenerating
degraded soils are critical to sustainable agrifood systems transformation –
requiring ISFM, efficient use of mineral and bio-based fertilizers, and sustainable
soil and water management practices. 1.2
OBJECTIVE
This report addresses the role of soil health in sustainable land productivity
growth as a foundation for improved food security in sub-Saharan Africa. It emphasizes soil fertility management approaches – including fertilizer use –
needed to support more productive and sustainable agrifood systems, and the
complementary need to improve farmers’ incentives to invest in soil health and
productivity. Soil fertility management and fertilizer use have generated a vast
literature, both institutional and academic (FAO, 2022b; World Bank, 2022b).7
Yet efforts to raise productivity and improve fertilizer use in SSA have achieved
only limited success. A new approach is therefore needed. Sustainable intensification will
be central to delivering economic, social, and environmental gains for smallholder farms and the region as a whole. Success will require nutrient manage
ment that increases crop productivity while ensuring efficient use of nutrients
at the higher fertilizer application rates of intensification models (Vanlauwe et
al., 2023). It will also depend on direct measures to address the economic con
straints smallholder farmers face. This report explores actions to mitigate further soil degradation and
rehabilitate those already degraded, and to incentivize fertilizer use that balanc
es long-term soil health and agricultural productivity with the immediate finan

REPORT STRUCTURE
This report is organized as follows. Section 1 describes the persistent food inse
curity and low agricultural productivity in sub-Saharan Africa, highlighting the
structural, environmental, and economic constraints that hinder sustainable
growth, the critical role of soil health in improving yields and nutrition, and the
evolution of soil fertility management approaches. Section 2 provides an over
view of soil patterns, soil health and soil degradation in sub-Saharan Africa. Section 3 examines the structural, agronomic, and economic challenges affect
ing fertilizer use and efficiency. Section 4 explores the growing awareness of and
opportunities to improve soil health, including the political economy of fertilizer
subsidies and developments in policies and programmes over the past 20 years. Section 5 sets out policy and investment options with scope for the next gener

2.1
A DIVERSITY OF SOIL TYPES AND QUALITY
Africa spans an exceptional range of climates and geology, and the continent’s
soils reflect this diversity (Jones et al., 2013). Weakly developed soils such as
Arenosols dominate the Sahara, Kalahari, Namib, and the Horn of Africa, encir
cling a central core of tropical soils. Ferralsols – strongly weathered and leached
soils associated with high rainfall and old land surfaces – are widespread in
Central, Eastern and Southern Africa. Gleysols, characterized by seasonal
waterlogging, dominate extensive wetlands such as along the Niger, Congo, and
Zambezi rivers. The Nile Valley, meanwhile, features vast stretches of heavy clay
soils classified as Vertisols (Jones et al., 2013), which have high shrink–swell
capacity and pose distinctive management challenges (IUSS Working Group
WRB, 2022). More than half of African land is unsuitable for rainfed agriculture. This 55 percent of the continent’s surface encompasses arid regions, salt pans,
sand dunes, rocky terrain, and steeply sloping land. These regions sustain
approximately 250 million inhabitants – representing 25 percent of the conti
nental population in 2014 – predominantly through nomadic pastoralism (Jones
et al., 2013). Some of these areas could potentially be brought into cultivation
through irrigation. Approximately 30 percent of African land, equivalent to 9 million km2,
has arable potential. Scarcely 16 percent of this area is high-quality soil, and
13 percent medium-grade, relatively free of major soil constraints to agriculture. Together, these categories represent approximately 8 percent of Africa’s land
mass. These areas support approximately 400 million people, or 40 percent of

largely free of nutrient deficiency or insufficient depth. They are suited to uses
ranging from crop cultivation, plantation agriculture, and forestry to aquaculture

across the continent, resulting in significant regional disparities in agricultural

Soil health challenges in SSA are compounded by farming practices that de
plete soil nutrients at a rate far exceeding their replenishment, particularly in
monoculture cereal systems where little crop residue remains in the field after
harvest. A 1995 study estimated nutrient losses over 25 years at approximately
700 kg of nitrogen, 100 kg of phosphorus, and 450 kg of potassium per hectare
across 100 million hectares of cultivated land (Sanchez and Leakey, 1997), with
average N depletion rates reaching 22 kg/ha annually between 1970 and 2000
in 37 African countries (Sanchez, 2002). In financial terms, the losses are stark:
SSA loses approximately USD 4 billion worth of soil nutrients annually through
nutrient mining (Vanlauwe et al., 2023), making it the only region with persistent
ly negative nutrient balances (Vanlauwe et al., 2023). This chronic depletion has
direct consequences in declining per capita food production on smallholder
farms (Hengl et al., 2017). Macronutrient losses vary considerably depending on the chemical
properties of each nutrient and its interactions with soil, water and wind. (For
detailed definitions and measures, see Section 3.5 and Annex 1.)
Farmers’ ability to replenish soil nutrients is constrained by a web of
interacting factors: the long time before investments in soil health pay off; land
tenure insecurity; liquidity and credit constraints (Vanlauwe et al., 2023); the
high cost of mineral fertilizers; and limited access to farm machinery. Demographic pressure on land compounds these factors, making traditional
restorative practices such as long fallow periods increasingly difficult to main
tain (Giller, 2020). Faced with these constraints, many farmers turn to land ex
pansion – often involving deforestation – rather than fallowing, seeking
short-term gains from temporarily more fertile soils. This search for fertility
through agricultural expansion accounts for roughly 90 percent of current glob
al deforestation (FAO et al., 2024). Continued low investment in soil fertility cannot be explained by mar
ket failures or information gaps alone – it also reflects the underlying heteroge
neity of smallholder farming systems. Differences in plot size, market access,
and livelihood orientation fundamentally shape both soil management decisions
and productivity outcomes. Subsistence farmers cultivating very small plots
face a distinct set of constraints: investments in soil fertility compete directly
with immediate food security needs, while uncertain returns, climate risk, poor
markets, and limited access to labour and credit amplify the cost of failure. This
is borne out empirically – nutrient balances are consistently negative on farms
where large areas are devoted to subsistence cereal production (Nkonya et al.,
2005), while positive balances appear on mixed farms where farmers apply
manure or cultivate high-value cash crops (Onduru et al., 2007; Vanlauwe et al.,
2015). Farm typology studies across SSA consistently identify patterns of varia
tion linked to plot size, resource endowment, and production objectives, con
firming that farmer type – rather than knowledge alone – determines soil
management outcomes (Chikowo et al., 2014). In this context, low fertilizer use
often reflects a rational response to risk rather than a lack of knowledge or
motivation – a distinction that is central to any accurate diagnosis of soil fertility
decline (Dercon and Christiaensen, 2011; Tittonell and Giller, 2013). THE SOIL CHALLENGES IN SUB-SAHARAN AFRICA

Fertilizer non-responsiveness adds another layer of complexity. A recent
study on maize and soybean found non-responsiveness ranging from
0 percent to 68 percent across sites and seasons, varying by crop and field
conditions such as irregular rainfall, soil texture, and nutrient imbalances. Soybean was most affected by low phosphorus and high silt content, while
non-responsiveness in maize was linked to high silt and cation imbalances
(Roobroeck et al., 2021). This wide variability underlines the limits of uniform
fertilizer recommendations and reinforces the case for more targeted, sitespecific approaches. Addressing these challenges thus requires approaches explicitly
grounded in the diversity of smallholder farming systems, rather than blanket
recommendations that assume homogeneity. Central to this are strategies such
as intercropping, crop rotation, and crop–livestock integration, not as transitional
steps toward input-intensive systems, but as core strategies for maintaining soil
health and managing production risk in the absence of external inputs. These
practices shape nutrient cycling, organic matter accumulation, and fertilizer re
sponsiveness in ways that differ fundamentally from monoculture or continuous
monocropping, which drive patterns of nutrient depletion and declining organic
matter. Effective targeting requires moving from regional-scale recommenda
tions to farm- and field-scale approaches, matched to site-specific biophysical
conditions, available resources, and household objectives (Vanlauwe et al., 2014). Cropping system choice is also closely bound up with farm size. Very
small plots often constrain the feasibility of crop rotation or fallowing, pushing
farmers toward repeated cultivation of the same crop and accelerating soil
degradation. Larger or more commercially oriented farms are better positioned
to diversify production, spread risk, and adopt soil-restoring practices whose
benefits materialize over time. Ultimately, soil health challenges are inseparable
from the production systems and land constraints that shape what farmers can
realistically do. Taken together, this evidence suggests that soil fertility is best under
stood as a conditional constraint: its importance for productivity growth is
undeniable, but the degree to which it actually limits productivity varies consid
erably depending on the farmer and the context. For smallholder subsistence farmers operating under tight economic and ecological constraints,
easing soil fertility bottlenecks requires coordinated responses that address
risk, incentives, and complementary investments alongside agronomic
considerations. 2.2
SOIL DEGRADATION UNDERMINES AGRICULTURAL LAND PRODUCTIVITY
AND FOOD SECURITY IN SSA
Soil degradation – the alteration of its physical, chemical, and biological proper
ties in ways that reduce its fertility and productive capacity – is a pervasive
problem across Africa, though estimates of the extent vary considerably. FAO
and ITPS (2015a) estimate that close to 500 million hectares of land in SSA are
affected, representing more than 20 percent of land in most countries in the
region.8 Other assessments put the share of degraded productive land at
65 percent (Mansourian and Berrahmouni, 2021), or even as much as
75–80 percent of the continent's cultivated area (AUDA-NEPAD, 2023), with
annual associated nutrient losses of 30 kg–60 kg of nutrients per hectare
(AUDA-NEPAD, 2023). A further estimate suggests that 46 percent of African

lands are degraded, potentially affecting the livelihoods of 485 million people
(AGNES, 2020). The divergence between these figures may reflect differences
in methodology, scope and definitions, but all point to a problem of substantial
and growing scale. Soil degradation manifests through four main processes: erosion,
organic matter depletion, nutrient depletion, and loss of soil biodiversity. Water
and wind erosion account for approximately 84 percent of all soil degradation,
with chemical degradation accounting for a further 12 percent and physical
degradation for the remaining 4 percent (FAO and ITPS, 2015a). Erosion and
physical degradation share many of the same drivers, including overgrazing,
deforestation, and unsustainable cultivation practices – such as complete crop
residue removal. Where soils are stripped of vegetation cover and organic
matter, they become more vulnerable to water and wind erosion, less able to
retain water and support plant growth, and less responsive to even appropriate
fertilizer use. Chemical degradation is associated with unbalanced or absent
fertilizer use (FAO, 2022a), as well as pollution from pesticide overuse or other
contamination. Expansion of agriculture into marginal areas and demographic pres
sures on existing farmland add further complexity (FAO, 2022a), contributing to
land fragmentation and insecure tenure arrangements that discourage longterm soil management. The consequences for productivity are severe. Yield losses on de
graded agricultural land range from moderate – approximately 2 percent over
several decades – to catastrophic, exceeding 50 percent in the worst-affected
areas, depending on crop, soil type, climate and production system (FAO,
2022a). Acidification, salinization, and desertification present additional, sig
nificant threats to soil health across SSA. Acid soils – covering up to half of the
region – reduce health through aluminium toxicity and phosphorus fixation,
while salinization driven by poor irrigation management and rising evaporation
disrupts soil structure and nutrient uptake. Desertification accelerates nutrient
loss and erosion, especially at the margins of arid and semi-arid zones,
diminishing soil productivity and resilience. Together, these processes com
pound existing degradation, further threatening crop yields, biodiversity, and
water regulation across the continent (Mesele et al., 2025). On degraded soils, nutrient deficiency cannot be addressed simply by
increasing application of mineral fertilizer. Low levels of soil organic matter im
pede nutrient uptake by plants, while poor water retention means that much of
any fertilizer applied is lost through leaching before the nutrients can be
absorbed by crops. Rehabilitation must therefore precede efficient fertilizer use. This process typically unfolds over several years and requires sustained exter
nal inputs, including both mineral and bio-based fertilizers, soil amendments,
and lime applications – alongside conservation practices. Approaches that rely
on mineral fertilizer alone, without first addressing the underlying soil condi
tions, are unlikely to achieve durable improvements in soil health or yields
(Vanlauwe et al., 2023). THE SOIL CHALLENGES IN SUB-SAHARAN AFRICA

Promoting fertilizer use is a central element of agricultural policy in many coun

Box 1) (Venkateswaran et al., 2025). Many countries use subsidies to make ferti

expenditures in national budgets (Zaveri, 2025). In Africa, nations allocate 14–26
percent of their agricultural budgets to fertilizer and input subsidies (Jayne et al.,
2018), with nitrogen constituting the bulk of those applied on African soils
(Sheahan and Barrett, 2017). Under- or over-subsidization of specific fertilizer
nutrient can lead to inefficient use (Sapkota and Bijay-Singh, 2025). Considering N, P, and K use together (see Figure 4), fertilizer use in

The role of fertilizers in soil fertility and agricultural development
Fertilizer refers to a chemical or natural substance or material used to provide
nutrients to plants, usually via application to the soil, but also to foliage or through
water by fertigation, hydroponics, or aquaponics operations (FAO, 2019). (For details
of different fertilizer types see Annex 2). Crop production depends on the adequate
availability of nutrients for plant growth and water to facilitate the conversion of
atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2) into organic matter through photosynthesis. It
requires various nutrients, including nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), potassium (K),
magnesium (Mg), sulphur (S), and micronutrients such as iron and zinc. Significant
quantities of nutrients are removed from agricultural land when crops are harvested
without replenishment (Falconnier et al., 2023). Fertilizer application has shaped agricultural development and land produc
tivity increases globally for decades. It has been estimated that almost half the people
in the world are fed because of the use of synthetic nitrogen fertilizer (Erisman et al.,
2008). The use of nitrogen as a fertilizer has doubled global rates of nitrogen fixation,
resulting in increases in crop yields of between 30 percent and 50 percent and lifting
billions of people out of food insecurity (Erisman et al., 2008; Stewart et al., 2005). Given the current estimates of soil depletion in SSA, combined with existing cropping
systems, these essential nutrients cannot be adequately replenished without the
application of fertilizers. When applied appropriately, they enhance soil fertility,
compensate for nutrient depletion, and significantly increase crop yields (FAO, 2019).

3.2
COSTS, MARKET STRUCTURE AND MARKET FAILURES LIMIT
FERTILIZER USE
The challenges of fertilizer use in sub-Saharan Africa are fundamentally rooted
in high prices, market structure and market failures, which give rise to a series
of interconnected supply and demand constraints examined in this section
(Abate, Abay and Spielman, 2020; Dillon and Barrett, 2017; Vanlauwe et al., 2023;
Isik, 2002). Countries that rely heavily on fertilizer imports are particularly
exposed to price volatility and supply disruptions – a vulnerability especially
pronounced across much of Africa, where even moderate price increases can
significantly reduce fertilizer use. African farmers who rely on fertilizers depend
heavily on imports from producers in the Persian Gulf and may face significantly
increased risks due to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz in 2026. A protracted
conflict would have serious implications for input trade, agricultural production
and food security across the continent (FAO, 2026a). 3.2.1
Mineral fertilizer prices well above the world average
The most immediate constraint is cost – fertilizers are expensive in sub-Saharan
Africa. Most of those used in SSA are imported (see Section 3.3), and fertilizer
prices are the highest in the world, up to four times higher than in Europe
(Hernandez and Torero, 2018). This disparity stems primarily from high logistical
costs, including international shipping to African ports, port handling, and inland
distribution through inefficient networks. These supply challenges are further
compounded by limited competition in a highly concentrated global fertilizer
industry, which may contribute to persistently high prices in SSA. Further detail
on price formation is provided in the following sections. 3.2.2
Extensive supply-side constraints
Numerous studies have highlighted supply-side constraints in fertilizer distribu
tion as a key economic factor limiting fertilizer use in most African countries
(Binswanger and Sillers, 1983; Dercon and Christiaensen, 2011; Karlan et al.,
2014). These constraints include high import prices and transport costs, con
tributing to high farm-gate prices and inconsistent availability (Hernandez et al.,
2018). Further supply-side challenges include inadequate infrastructure, limited
market competition, inefficient distribution systems, and insufficient private
sector investment. Evidence from the green revolution, particularly in India,
demonstrates the importance of research and development, and of crucial

Significant demand-side limitations
Fertilizer use is also constrained by several demand-side factors, including in
adequate information on soil types and fertilizer recommendations, farmer
perception of fertilizer quality, inadequate packaging sizes, low returns on in
vestment, and limited access to agricultural extension services. Farmers use little fertilizer when returns are low – when crop prices are
too low relative to fertilizer costs, or when production risks are too high. Farmers
in remote areas may not be able to sell surplus production profitably because
local consumers have limited purchasing power and nearby markets are small. This problem persists even when people in these areas face hunger and food
insecurity, because poor roads, high transport costs, and weak market connec
tions prevent food needs from translating into actual market demand that farm
ers can respond to. Figure 9 illustrates an important pattern: countries with larger nonagricultural sectors use significantly more fertilizer per hectare. Since a larger
non-agricultural sector generates growing urban demand for food, this suggests
that urbanization and economic diversification – not agriculture itself – help to
drive fertilizer demand. Simply put, farmers invest in fertilizers when it is profit
able, and reliable markets and a strong non-farm economy play important roles
in making that possible. Niger provides an example of this dynamic. With 83 percent of its
population living in rural areas – one of the highest agricultural dependency
rates in the world – Niger uses only 3 kg of fertilizer per hectare, among the
lowest rates anywhere. Without sufficient urban demand and economic diversi
fication, farmers lack the market incentives to invest in productivity-enhancing
inputs – a dynamic in which functional input, credit and output markets play a
major role. Several studies show that the considerable variations in returns on
fertilizer use in Africa can be explained in part by soil type. There is robust
evidence that low soil fertility and soil acidity can render mineral fertilizers un
profitable (Marenya and Barrett, 2009; Burke, Jayne and Black, 2017). Abate,
Abay and Spielman (2020) note that different types and brands of chemical
fertilizers contain varying types and levels of nutrients, implying that their prof
itability depends on specific soil nutrient requirements and application condi
tions. In most cases, soil testing and associated agronomic assessments are
usually costly and inaccessible to smallholder farmers across most of the conti
nent, and the spatial resolution of soil tests remains quite low (Carletto et al.,
2017). Consequently, farmers may rely on inaccurate proxies for their soil prop
erties (Berazneva et al., 2018). Innovations in soil mapping and testing technologies offer potential
solutions to the lack of soil property information, though these are still not widely

practices. Infrastructure constraints such as outdated equipment, unreliable

sufficient training in fertilizer quality control, fragmented regulatory frameworks,
low levels of inspection, and limited enforcement of existing laws. Addressing
these issues requires strengthening regulatory capacity across the supply
chain, implementing pre-export verification systems and improving storage and

A World Bank review published around the time of the fertilizer price peak in
mid-2022 underlined challenges in the physical quality of fertilizers, such as
granule integrity and packaging. While these issues do not appear to reduce
fertilizer efficacy, they can make application more difficult and negatively influ
ence farmer perceptions of quality. The review noted that high and rising ferti
lizer prices – which by early 2022 had already surpassed the peaks of the
2007–2008 food price crisis – could alter the incentives for adulteration and
counterfeiting. This suggests that fertilizer quality is dynamic and responds to
market conditions. It is therefore crucial to continuously collect data on both
fertilizer quality and farmer beliefs, as these may also change in response to
price fluctuations and perceived shortages (Michelson, Gourlay and Wollburg,
2022). Smallholder farmers’ negative experiences with and perceptions of
fertilizer quality may constitute another constraint to adoption, creating a com
plex dynamic that affects farmers' willingness to invest in agricultural inputs
(Michelson et al., 2021). Farmers rely on multiple observable signals to assess
quality, including the physical appearance of the fertilizer, packaging condition,
retail location, brand reputation, and observed crop yields. These perceptions
are often reinforced by media coverage of adulteration cases, further complicat
ing efforts to build trust in the market. Evidence from the United Republic of
Tanzania demonstrates a disconnect between actual fertilizer quality and farm
ers' perceptions. While available fertilizers typically meet national quality stand
ards, farmers maintain significant scepticism about product authenticity
(Michelson et al., 2021). This perception gap is reflected in purchasing behaviour:
when farmers receive credible information about fertilizer quality, particularly
regarding unobservable characteristics such as nitrogen content, their willing
ness to pay increases by approximately 50 percent. Without such information,
farmers remain widely suspicious of the agronomic quality of the fertilizer in the
market, suggesting a substantial information asymmetry (Michelson et al., 2021). Poor storage conditions and potential adulteration during repackag
ing may also discourage farmers from investing in fertilizers. To protect consum
ers from adulterated products and reduce quality control challenges and the
risk of corruption (Chianu, Chianu and Mairura, 2012a), many sub-Saharan
African countries prohibit fertilizer repackaging. However, packaging size
presents an additional barrier to access and adoption for smaller-scale agricul
tural operations (Chianu, Chianu and Mairura, 2012a). Standard 50 kg bags,
mandated by regulation or entrenched by commercial habit, are often too large
and too costly for smallholder farmers. Smaller packages could better meet the
time-based needs of such resource-constrained farmers, though they come at
a higher cost per unit of weight. Farmers’ fertilizer use may also be impeded by informational or knowl
edge barriers. Ineffective agricultural extension services, for example, may
hinder knowledge dissemination and, consequently, the adoption of improved
technology. Farmers’ organizations can serve as one mechanism for delivering
agricultural extension services by promoting use of fertilizers, high-quality
seeds, and yield-enhancing practices. Moreover, they have the potential to
contribute to education, innovation, and market access. Such organizations may
rely on support from governments and other agencies, however, and may lack
the technical, managerial or leadership capacity to address these roles effec
tively. They may also be ill-equipped to support farmers constrained by infra
structure challenges (e.g. lack of irrigation, storage facilities, and feeder roads)
or limited financial access (Bizikova et al., 2020). FERTILIZER UNDERUSED, OFTEN MISUSED IN SSA

Beyond knowledge and organizational constraints, financial flows and timing
further limit fertilizer adoption. A farmer’s cash flow from agricultural income
does not often coincide with input expenditure cycles, making it difficult to pur
chase fertilizer at the appropriate time. Farmers typically sell their crops at
harvest time when market prices are lowest yet must purchase fertilizer at the
start of the planting season when they may face credit and liquidity constraints. This mismatch particularly affects smallholder farmers. Evidence from four
countries – Malawi, Nigeria, Uganda, and the United Republic of Tanzania –
shows that credit use for fertilizer, pesticide or seed purchases is extremely low,
with only 6 percent of farmers on average using any form of credit to buy inputs. Modern inputs are primarily financed through cash from non-farm activities and
crop sales (Adjognon, Liverpool-Tasie and Reardon, 2017). Moreover, fertilizers are often perceived as risk-increasing inputs:
while they can enhance average crop yields, they also amplify yield variability
under changing conditions such as rainfall and pest prevalence (Finger, 2012;
Rajsic, Weersink and Gandorfer, 2009). As discussed in Section 2.1, this risk
dynamic varies considerably across farm types. Semi-commercial and commer
cial farmers operating in well-connected markets face a fundamentally different
risk calculus than subsistence smallholders, for whom fertilizer investment often
competes directly with immediate food security needs and where the absence
or inadequate performance of input, credit and output markets and extension
services makes the cost of failure prohibitively high (Chianu, Chianu and Mairura,
2012a; Bizikova et al., 2020). Cash crop value chains such as cocoa, coffee and
cotton offer models of contractual arrangements to ease smallholder liquidity
constraints for the purchase of fertilizer and other inputs, often on credit (Tsakok
and Guedegbe, 2019; Tefft, 2010). Beyond soil properties, returns to fertilizer investment vary systemat
ically with farm size, market connectivity, and agroecological endowment. Where fertilizer has delivered sustained productivity gains – such as in parts of
Kenya, Ethiopia, and Nigeria – positive outcomes have typically been concen
trated in better-endowed zones or among farmers with reliable market access
and adequate infrastructure and services (e.g. roads, extension and credit). In Nigeria, fertilizer use and yield improvements have been markedly higher in
well-connected states than in regions lacking infrastructure and market access
(Takeshima and Liverpool-Tasie, 2015). These patterns confirm that fertilizer use
in SSA is often of limited economic benefit once uncertainty, transaction costs,
and a lack of infrastructure investments are accounted for – and that effective
interventions require distinguishing farmers by plot size, agroecology, and de
gree of market integration. The rationality of low fertilizer use under structural constraints is
well-documented. In Ethiopia, fertilizer application rates dropped significantly
when farmers faced risks of a poor harvest due to rainfall failure. This was not
because fertilizer was unprofitable on average, but because the cost of a failed
harvest under liquidity constraints outweighed the expected gains (Dercon and
Christiaensen, 2011). Moreover, experiments in Ghana confirmed that when
credit and insurance were made available, farmers substantially increased fer
tilizer use, indicating that structural constraints, rather than limited knowledge,
were the determining factor (Karlan et al., 2014). Economic analyses reinforce
this picture: in Zambia, fertilizer was profitable at commercial prices for only
37 percent of urea users and as few as 8 percent of those applying basal fertiliz
er on acidic soils – meaning low use often reflected a correct assessment of

returns (Burke, Jayne and Black, 2017). Similarly in Nigeria, marginal returns to
nitrogen on maize decline sharply beyond an application rate of 50 kg/ha
meaning that additional fertilizer beyond a modest threshold yielded diminish
ing economic returns and made those applications unprofitable for many small
holders (Adjognon, Liverpool-Tasie and Reardon, 2017). Finally, a substantial structural constraint is the price environment
itself. Farm-gate fertilizer prices remain high across much of SSA, while food
crop prices are significantly lower and often more variable than those in other
areas (Maître d'Hôtel and Le Cotty, 2018) – including in Asian countries where
the green revolution succeeded (Hernandez et al., 2018; Pingali, 2023). Farmers'
fertilizer demand often depends on their ability to sell increased agricultural
production at remunerative prices, emphasizing the importance of farmerconsumer market connections. While better infrastructure and logistics can
expand market access (Benson and Mogues, 2018), as already discussed,
improvements in connectivity alone are insufficient where the underlying price
environment renders fertilizer investment unprofitable. The classic characteri
zation of the "poor but efficient" farmer remains apt in many SSA contexts:
constrained by poverty, risk, and missing markets, smallholders optimize for
survival rather than maximum yield (Dercon and Christiaensen, 2011). Under
these conditions, maximizing food security – by preserving cash as a buffer
against crop failure – can be a more rational strategy than investing in expensive
inputs with uncertain returns. 3.3

regional production capacity, and significant — though largely unrealized —

3.4
EMERGING BUT STILL LIMITED MARKETS FOR BIO-BASED FERTILIZERS
Bio-based fertilizers – encompassing both organic fertilizers and biological
fertilizers – represent a viable alternative to mineral inputs, and have a particu
larly important role to play in Africa over the long term, given the continent’s high
rate of soil organic carbon (SOC) degradation (Mącik, Gryta and Frąc, 2020). Both organic fertilizers, derived from plant and animal residues, and
biological fertilizers that incorporate microorganisms fixing atmospheric nitro
gen and enhancing nutrient availability, offer broader soil health benefits than
just providing nutrients – improving soil structure, supporting microbial activity,
and building long-term health. A farmer’s decision to use them is nonetheless
influenced by socioeconomic factors including land and labour availability, op
portunity costs, the degree of crop-livestock integration, and the cost of such
bio-based inputs (Vanlauwe et al., 2023).

The African organic fertilizer market is projected to grow from an estimated
USD 560 million in 2025 to USD 990 million by 2029 (Mordor Intelligence, 2024). This growth is fuelled in part by substantial expansion in organic farming, the
benefits of organic fertilizers in conventional agriculture beyond the provision of
N, P and K, and rising mineral fertilizer prices that have prompted some farmers
to shift towards organic alternatives. Organic agriculture in Africa has grown
from around 50 000 hectares in 2000 to approximately 2.03 million hectares in
2019, though the continent still has the smallest share of organically farmed land
of any world region (Statista, 2024). Africa’s organic fertilizer market is segment
ed by type (i.e. microorganisms and organic residues), application, and geogra
phy, with key markets comprising South Africa, Egypt and Ethiopia (Mordor
Intelligence, 2024). The global market for biological fertilizer is expanding in several
advanced economies, supported by tax incentives, input subsidies, as well as
market development and financial support. SSA countries will need to make a
similar strategic shift towards biological fertilizer in order to realize the economic
and environmental potential of bio-inputs observed in regions such as Latin
America (Bullor et al., 2024). Bio-inputs are a central element in the transition to
sustainable agrifood systems enabling the conservation of biodiversity, increas
ing soil health, and enhancing agricultural efficiency. The bio-inputs market in
Latin America, growing at approximately 15 percent annually, reflects their role
in reducing farmers' reliance on costly conventional agrochemicals and in main
taining access to highly regulated export markets. However, realizing this poten
tial requires overcoming constraints including the need for specialized cold
storage and distribution infrastructure, and the establishment of robust national
regulatory frameworks to ensure product quality and build farmer trust (Bullor
et al., 2024). In SSA, the potential of biological fertilizer products has been largely
untapped due to inadequate market development, weak regulatory frameworks,
poorly enforced quality control standards, and limited farmer knowledge and
skills in using these inputs. These challenges have contributed to unregulated
production and an influx of commercial biofertilizers of questionable quality –
undermining farmer confidence and hampering adoption across the continent
(Raimi, Roopnarain and Adeleke, 2021). Addressing these barriers requires
policy commitment to train extension agents, strengthen standards and en
forcement, and mobilize private sector investment and compliance with estab
lished regulations. Such steps could help to address the high rate of degradation of
SOC – the crucial carbon component in soils (Dugué, Andrieu and Bakker, 2024). Living inocula of microorganisms that fix atmospheric nitrogen and enhance
nutrient availability can be reused from one season to the next – an inexpensive
practice widely used in India and Latin America that requires less technology
and knowledge than high-precision fertilization (Umesha, Singh and Singh,
2018). Such efforts should, however, be accompanied by quality and safety
assessments to ensure that bio-based products meet agronomic standards and
do not introduce contaminants or pathogens into soils and food systems. FERTILIZER UNDERUSED, OFTEN MISUSED IN SSA

3.5
SOIL, AGRONOMIC, AND ECONOMIC CONSTRAINTS ON FERTILIZER
EFFICIENCY
The efficiency of mineral fertilizer use in SSA is shaped by a variety of interlock
ing agronomic, environmental and economic factors. Fundamental to these are
soil characteristics, agricultural practices, and the fertilizer type, quality, amount
and timing of application. In general, deep soils rich in organic matter content with good water
retention offer greater productivity and make fertilizers more effective, as more
nutrients are available for optimal crop growth. Africa’s more common sandy or
ferritic soils, by contrast, are frequently acidic – whether naturally or as a result
of poor soil management – limiting macro- and micronutrient uptake by crops. Soil acidity affects approximately 25 percent of soils in Africa (FAO and ITPS,
2015b),16 representing one of the main biophysical constraints on fertilizer
response. Farming practices significantly compound these soil constraints, with
nutrient mining a widespread concern across the continent. This process –
characterised by an imbalance between soil nutrient inputs and outputs –
depletes nutrient reserves and SOC, contributing to erosion, acidification, and
the release of CO2 and nitrous oxide into the atmosphere. In SSA, this process is
driven primarily by the chronic underuse of mineral fertilizers, leaving essential
nutrients unreplenished (Vanlauwe et al., 2023). This stands in contrast to con
ditions in other regions, where overuse of mineral fertilizers drives acidification,
soil pollution,17 water quality hazards including eutrophication, and risks to hu
man health such as elevated nitrates in drinking water. Improving nitrogen use efficiency will become increasingly important
in SSA’s agrifood systems. Globally, nitrogen use is inefficient in that plants do
not make adequate use of the applied nitrogen, implying that the increase in
yield per unit of nutrient applied is not as high as it could be. Less than half of the
nitrogen supplied to crops is utilized on average, and research suggests that
nitrogen applied to wheat, rice, and maize could be reduced by 14–29 percent
worldwide while maintaining yields (West et al., 2014). Greater efficiency is
achievable through changes in fertilizer timing, placement, rate and type (West
et al., 2014). For African producers, improvements in nutrient use efficiency
would directly reduce input costs – a significant consideration given the price
constraints explored earlier (Vanlauwe et al., 2023). The efficiency of fertilizer use in SSA is further complicated by diverse
cropping systems and by the geographical and economic conditions facing
producers. Maize, for example, is agronomically highly responsive to nitrogen
fertilizer, and its cultivation is associated in many places with greater mineral
fertilizer use. From an economic point of view, however, whether that use is prof
itable depends on a range of factors beyond agronomy and affecting producer
prices – including road infrastructure and transport costs, fertilizer and other
input prices, output market prices, and market structure. 16Acidic soils are deficient in phosphorus, calcium and magnesium, and may have toxic
levels of aluminium. 17Between 30 percent and 50 percent of mineral fertilizer nutrients end up contaminating
groundwater or volatilizing into the air (Chojnacka, Moustakas and Witek-Krowiak,
2020).

4.1
PRODUCTION POTENTIAL IN HEALTHY SOILS
Approximately 30 percent of arable land in Africa has good agronomic potential,
suitable for intensification through mineral or bio-based fertilizers (FAO and
ITPS, 2015a). In many humid, sub-humid, and some semi-arid areas, a “doubly
green” revolution is technically feasible – improving both the environment and
agricultural output simultaneously.18 Assuming there is water and organic mat
ter in the soil, using more fertilizer in an efficient manner would help to increase
yields and output. Mineral fertilizers are needed to reach yield potential. In case studies
across a range of SSA countries, Falconnier et al. (2023) found that maize yield
potential ranged from 3.5–11.9 tonnes/ha (with a median of 6.5 tonnes/ha),
implying median N uptake of 113 kg/ha. They argue that N, P and K needs at
these yield levels in smallholder systems cannot be met through biological ni
trogen fixation, such as by legumes, and animal manure alone (Falconnier et al.,
2023). Nevertheless, from a nutrient balance perspective, mineral fertilizer
remains necessary in these cases to improve soil fertility and increase yields in
the short term (Falconnier et al., 2023; Vanlauwe et al., 2023), even when apply
ing agroecological principles to increase nutrient availability. 4.2
THE POLITICAL ECONOMY AND LIMITATIONS OF FERTILIZER SUBSIDIES
Low fertilizer use rates and the need to boost agricultural production have led to
calls over the last two decades for African governments to take more action. Three successive regional declarations – the Comprehensive Africa Agriculture
Development Programme’s (CAADP) Maputo Declaration of 2003, the 2006
Abuja Declaration, and the 2014 Malabo Declaration – each committed member
states to increasing fertilizer use and agricultural productivity, yet there has
been limited impact. 18This differs from the green revolution, which historically focused on agricultural
output (Conway, 1997). Growing opportunities

CAADP committed African governments to double agricultural productivity by
focusing on the provision of improved inputs. The Abuja Declaration declared
fertilizer a strategic commodity and resolved that African Union
member states should promote its use through targeted subsidies (AUC, 2006). That declaration was most specific, targeting fertilizer consumption of 50 kg/ha
by 2015, against an SSA average of just 8 kg/ha in 2006 (AUC, 2006). It set out
interventions at regional and country levels – including policy and regulatory
frameworks, targeted subsidies, and improved access to complementary inputs
– and was reinforced in 2014 by the Malabo Declaration in which African leaders
affirmed their CAADP commitments and called for smart subsidies carefully
targeted to smallholder agriculture (AUC, 2014). Some countries responded by revising their fertilizer policies and
regulations (among them Burkina Faso, Ghana, Kenya, Mali, Mozambique,
Rwanda, Uganda, the United Republic of Tanzania, and Zambia) (Abate,
Abay and Spielman, 2020), but many still lack a coherent fertilizer policy
(AGRA, 2019). For most, subsidies have been the preference in policy and
programmes. Fertilizer and input subsidies in Africa are estimated at 14–26 percent
of national budget allocations to agriculture between 2011 and 2014 (Jayne et al.,
2018), a substantial share of agricultural spending in some of SSA’s biggest
economies. Despite varying programme designs across countries, crops and
years (see Box 2), their overall impact on productivity and poverty outcomes has
been disappointing. Most studies in SSA show that fertilizer subsidies do not significantly
impact production, land productivity or farmers’ incomes. They are generally
costly and poorly targeted – particularly in landlocked countries (Arslan et al.,
2022; Maître d'Hôtel and Issoufou, 2018) – and often subject to rent-seeking
(Holden and Lunduka, 2012). Malawi’s subsidy experience is regularly cited,
though it remains contested in terms of both implementation and outcomes
(Denning et al., 2009; Dorward and Chirwa, 2011; Sachs, 2012; Jayne and Rashid,
2013). More fundamentally, the heterogeneity of smallholder farming systems
and soil conditions demands targeted rather than blanket recommendations –
a reality that broad subsidy programmes have struggled to accommodate
(Vanlauwe et al., 2023).19
The political economy of these policies and programmes also adds
another layer of complexity. In SSA, fertilizer subsidies are widely believed to be
popular among voters, making them attractive to politicians seeking to secure
or retain power – even though evidence for this effect is mixed (Mason, Jayne
and Van de Walle, 2017). Even the best-designed fertilizer policies and subsidy
programmes are difficult to implement and can produce unintended
consequences. The lesson from this experience is that SSA governments cannot
achieve productivity goals by simply increasing volumes of fertilizer distributed
or public funds allocated (Abate, Abay and Spielman, 2020). More effective,
holistic policies and programmes are needed that improve agricultural produc
tivity while carefully considering socioeconomic, agronomic, and sustainability

Public support for fertilizer use in SSA has taken three broad forms, broadly in line
with the evolution of agricultural policies (Lehe et al., 2025). The first entails state-led fertilizer marketing, characterized by universal or nearuniversal fertilizer price subsidies, with public agencies prominent in procurement,
pricing, and distribution. Prevalent across much of Africa from independence in the
1960s to the structural adjustment programme era in the 1980s, these policies
increased fertilizer use among farmers – particularly in the later years of this period
(Eicher, 1995; Byerlee and Eicher, 1997). The design and implementation of these
policies have, however, been shown to have high fiscal cost, with market-distorting
effects and significant rent-seeking (Jayne and Jones, 1997; Morris et al., 2007;
Yamano and Arai, 2010). The second is market-oriented reform, in which governments introduced
more market-led fertilizer procurement and distribution mechanisms. These reforms
have varied considerably in scope and depth across countries, and their results were
mixed – and often controversial (Jayne et al., 2002, 2003; Minot and Benson, 2009). The third category covers policy and programme modification, aimed at
improving targeting and mitigating the unintended consequences – budgetary,
environmental, and market – of earlier approaches. In the late 2010s, Nigeria intro

fertilizer subsidies through electronic vouchers. Other countries, including Malawi,
Mozambique, Rwanda, Zambia, and Zimbabwe, have been following this lead with
e-wallet and e-voucher schemes. The effectiveness of these innovations and smart
subsidy programmes will depend on the institutional and political contexts in which
they are introduced (Jayne et al., 2018). Despite this evolution, the evidence increasingly points to the limits of
fertilizer subsidies as a standalone tool to sustainably improve productivity. Subsidies
consistently fail to address the underlying constraints that drive under-use: poor soil
health reduces returns to standard fertilizer packages; rainfed systems make fertilizer
investments weather-dependent and risky; inefficient output markets keep crop
prices too low relative to input costs; and underdeveloped financial markets prevent
farmers from purchasing complementary inputs or insuring against production risk

crowd out private input market development. These findings point toward a reorientation of public spending, rather than

address the underlying constraints more effectively – and to make any remaining

FROM ABUJA TO NAIROBI: CONSENSUS ON INTEGRATED SOIL HEALTH
Over the past two decades, Africa’s political commitment to fertilizers, and soil
fertility more broadly, has undergone a significant shift. Starting from a narrower
focus on boosting mineral fertilizer consumption in the 2006 Abuja Declaration,
the highest-level continental commitments now take in a broader, more integrat
ed vision of soil health and sustainable agrifood systems, culminating in the
2024 Nairobi Declaration. The Africa Fertilizer Summit held in Abuja, Nigeria in 2006 identified
the critical need to increase fertilizer use to stimulate agricultural productivity
growth and reverse the trend of soil nutrient depletion. Rooted in the productiv
ist vision of the East Asian Miracle three decades earlier (World Bank, 1993), the
Abuja Declaration treated mineral fertilizer as the primary lever for intensifica
tion and in delivering an “African Green Revolution”. There was little mention of
soil health, nor of the possible negative health and environmental impacts of the
green revolution in Asia (Pingali, 2012). As explored in Section 4.2, the results
were limited, and even with the reinforcement of the Malabo Declaration in 2014,
fertilizer use in SSA remained well below target. Moreover, the structural con
straints on smallholder investment in inputs largely went unaddressed.

The food and climate crises that have deepened since 2006 have had a remark
able impact on the policymaking context in Africa – and the thinking on sustain
able agrifood systems. Eighteen years after Abuja, the 2024 Africa Fertilizer and
Soil Health Summit (AFSH), convened in Nairobi, Kenya, explicitly reframed the
agenda, as an opportunity for “decisive steps towards sustainably increasing
agricultural productivity to reduce hunger and malnutrition, improve livelihoods,
and adapt to the impacts of climate change” (African Union, 2024a; AUDA-
NEPAD, 2024; African Union, 2024b). These words marked a significant political
evolution: Not only was soil health now explicitly embraced in the 2024 summit
title, but climate change – entirely absent from the 2006 declaration – was now
central to the agenda. While the 2006 declaration had briefly acknowledged the
environment, there had been no mention of sustainability or sustainable
approaches. The shift was clear in the Nairobi Declaration – which balances the productivity narrative with convincing evidence on the importance of soil health, soil
nutrients and soil fertility – and the Africa Fertilizer and Soil Health Action Plan:
2024–2034.20 Crucially, the action plan acknowledges that “mineral fertilizers
alone are inadequate to reverse land degradation and sustainably increase the
productivity of Africa’s soils” (African Union, 2024d). ISFM and sustainable soil
and water management are set out as the framework for future investment.21
Leaders recognized the integrated nature of Africa’s agricultural sub-sectors
and soil health concerns, and the need to prioritize integrated soil and water
conservation and management at watershed, landscape, and catchment level. In the spirit of the Africa Common Position on Food Systems (African Union,
2023), the declaration articulates a comprehensive aspiration to improve food
security and nutrition, promote inclusive economic growth, and ensure equita
ble and balanced territorial development while ensuring environmental sustain
ability and resilience. The declaration also broadened the goal from crop
productivity and profitability to encompass socioeconomic and environmental
sustainability, considering climate change adaptation and mitigation, rehabilita
tion of degraded land, and restoration and maintenance of ecosystem services,
including biodiversity. The Nairobi Declaration reiterates that increasing fertiliz
er use in Africa remains a valid goal to be achieved in a way that supports soil
health and environmental resilience. The measure of progress will lie in how
effectively these commitments are translated into coordinated actions. The 2025 Kampala CAADP Declaration moved swiftly to embed this
agenda within the continent’s principal framework for translating agricultural
undertakings into national investment plans, reaffirming core commitments to
investing in soil fertility and health as the cornerstone of sustainable agrifood
system transformation. African Union member states pledged to scale up in
vestments in ISFM and promote climate-smart and regenerative practices
alongside the enhanced use of bio-based and mineral fertilizers in an environ
mentally sustainable manner. Critical to this effort is recognition of the necessity
of improving farmer access to quality, affordable fertilizers through strength
ened functional input systems, regional harmonization of standards, and boost
ing local production capacity, while mitigating post-harvest losses and soil
