Improving soil health and sustainably boosting food production in SSA require
more than better access to fertilizer. They demand a coordinated policy
response across four interconnected objectives: improving soil health and
fertility; increasing fertilizer availability; improving fertilizer access and
affordability; and strengthening producers’ incentives to invest in their land. These mutually reinforcing priorities reflect the analysis in this report and should
be considered together as part of an integrated soil health and fertilizer policy
framework. They are grounded in the 2024 Nairobi Declaration and support the
Africa Fertilizer and Soil Health Action Plan: 2024–2034 in the aim to drive the
sustainable transformation of agrifood systems across the region. Secure land tenure is a critical prerequisite for implementing most
agricultural investment projects in SSA (Cotula and Toulmin, 2008), as it is
fundamental to attracting finance. Land serves as a key asset that can be used
as security for loans, enabling farmers to access credit for the expansion of
production, the purchase of equipment, fertilizers, and soil improvement inputs. Without secure land rights, farmers face significant barriers to obtaining capital
from banks and other lenders, limiting their ability to invest in productivityenhancing measures and ultimately undermining food security and livelihoods. In short, land tenure determines not only where to invest but also whether to
invest, as financial institutions and insurers are unlikely to provide credit or
coverage without clear and enforceable land rights. Policy and investment
options

5.1
IMPROVING SOIL HEALTH AND SOIL FERTILITY
Strategies to prioritize soil health and fertility must be carefully tailored to con
text. Key considerations include climate variations – distinguishing between dry
and humid conditions – soil condition, the interactions between crop and live
stock systems, and the potential for integrating agroforestry. Effective strate
gies demand nuanced understanding of local soil needs and strategic use of
targeted tools and instruments to achieve comprehensive soil health
objectives. There is broad consensus on the need for sustainability in soil fertility,
drawing efficiently on both bio-based and mineral sources of nutrients. The
Africa Fertilizer and Soil Health Action Plan: 2024–2034 proposes ISFM, while
agroecological approaches have been recommended by a range of global insti
tutions (HLPE, 2019; CFS, 2021b). Diverse actors across SSA emphasize different
aspects of this broad agenda. Some advocate a transition without chemical in
puts, focusing on the bio-based sector; others argue for a balanced approach,
particularly in areas where mineral fertilizer use remains low, and where these
inputs could complement nutrients provided by agroecological practices such
as the use of legumes, manure, biofertilizers, biostimulants, and cover crops. On
degraded soils, where mineral fertilizer use is least efficient, restoring soil
organic matter and improving water retention are prerequisites, as discussed in
Section 2.2. These approaches take time to generate returns – often represent
ing a major constraint for small-scale producers – which underlines the need for
policies and incentives that support investment in soil health, not just access to
fertilizers (Vanlauwe et al., 2023). Support for localized soil testing facilities, along with the promotion
and supply of related products such as lime for acidic soils and crop- and
soil-specific fertilizer blends, is an important aspect of delivering localized solu
tions at scale. Improving producers’ awareness of alternative tools – including
portable soil and plant sensors and soil management applications – and of the
benefits of different production practices, is a relevant complement in many
countries and systems. These efforts work best when combined with incentives
for agribusinesses to promote and distribute supplementary products, ideally
as part of a bundled package that includes soil and plant analysis alongside
other technology-based services. Recent success stories in localized soil management taken to scale
include the AKILIMO site-specific fertilizer recommendation portal for cassava,
developed by the African Cassava Agronomy Initiative, and the SOILS
Consortium Space to Place programme in Ethiopia, funded by USAID (Vanlauwe
et al., 2023). The FAO Soil Mapping for Resilient Agrifood Systems Programme
(SoilFER), implemented in Ghana, Kenya, Mozambique, Tunisia, and Zambia,
illustrates the potential of an integrated institutional capacity development ap
proach. It combines soil surveys, national soil information systems, strength
ened soil laboratories, and farmer-focused extension services, through the
Global Soil Doctors Programme. These models demonstrate that strategic in
vestment in localized soil infrastructure can meaningfully improve deci
sion-making on fertilizer use and sustainable soil management (FAO, 2024c). High-quality soil health advisory services that deliver practical, accessible infor
mation help to build producer trust and improve uptake. Strengthening soil science and plant nutrition knowledge across the
full range of stakeholders – from farmers and extension agents to researchers
and agribusiness professionals – is an important foundation for sustainable

agriculture. This requires expanding and upgrading soil science education
through formal institutions and lifelong learning, including informal education in
local languages (AUC, 2023). Proven models suitable for scaling up include the
Accelerating Impacts of CGIAR Climate Research for Africa (AICCRA) and the
Centre of Excellence for Soil and Fertilizer Research in Africa (CESFRA) at
Mohammed VI Polytechnic University in Morocco. Soil fertility investments may be more effective when differentiated or
targeted by farm type. Subsistence farmers with limited land and poor market
access face fundamentally different constraints to those of semi-commercial or
commercial producers, and uniform approaches will consistently underperform
relative to targeted ones. For smallholder subsistence farmers cultivating less
than one hectare primarily for family consumption, programmes that reduce risk
and build economic resilience – such as drought insurance, cash transfers,
productive safety nets, and access to credit – should precede or accompany
fertilizer promotion, rather than implicitly assuming that the necessary enabling
conditions for fertilizer use are already in place. For emerging commercial farm
ers with larger plots and better market connectivity, the priority shifts toward
improved market access, price stabilization, and tailored fertilizer blends or
credit programmes that make intensification economically viable. Sequencing
and targeting interventions in this way is not just more equitable – it is more
likely to generate sustained productivity gains. 5.2
INCREASE THE PRODUCTION AND AVAILABILITY OF FERTILIZERS
FROM SSA
The second policy objective concerns increasing the availability of both mineral
and bio-based fertilizers in SSA. This could be pursued through four comple
mentary approaches: (i) boosting local production for domestic and regional
supply; (ii) improving incentives and reducing risks for private sector invest
ments (e.g. green hydrogen-based fertilizers22 and bio-based production);
(iii) addressing structural market inefficiencies and strengthening competition
to achieve economies of scale, including through improved transport infrastruc
ture and reduced trade-related administrative burdens; and (iv) prioritizing
foundational public investments to improve overall sector performance. Promoting investment in production and adoption of bio-based ferti
lizers in particular could have a significant impact on soil health and crop pro
ductivity. Where farmer demand for fertilizers remains unmet, a fertilizer
production policy would seek to remove barriers to national and regional trade
and offer incentives to increase the supply and improve the price competitive
ness of African-produced fertilizers. Assuming there is unmet demand from
farmers, a comprehensive policy could also aim to ease market constraints
hampering producer profitability and to incentivize the production and distribu
tion of bio-based and mineral fertilizers. Rural fertilizer markets in SSA do not function efficiently, suggesting
that strategic interventions are necessary. These include measures to promote
market competition, mitigate risks for private investors, improve distribution
systems, and strengthen private sector participation in the fertilizer value chain. Investment in enabling public goods – such as roads, storage facilities, informa
tion systems, and extension services – is often a critical prerequisite to

well-functioning markets, creating the favourable economic environment in
which both locally produced and imported fertilizers can reach farmers
efficiently. Strategic market mechanisms and financial instruments can address
supply chain inefficiencies and price volatility directly. The African Trade
Exchange Platform, a business-to-business and business-to-government
e-commerce platform, was launched in 2022, exemplifies this approach by
aggregating continental demand to negotiate competitive prices and enable
access to affordable fertilizers, creating economies of scale and reducing trans
action costs. Similarly, the Africa Fertilizer Financing Mechanism (AFFM), a fund
established in 2007 and administered by the African Development Bank Group
(AfDB), provides critical financial support to enhance pan-African agricultural
productivity by promoting fertilizer use. Combining AFFM credit guarantees
with the African Trade Exchange Platform has the potential to mitigate some of
the market failures observed in Africa’s fertilizer market. Realizing the full potential of these mechanisms, however requires
substantial public investment in research and development and in innovative
financing instruments – such as long-maturity lines of credit – channelled
through microfinance institutions and first-tier commercial banks with the
explicit aim of improving soil fertility and fertilizer use efficiency among small
holders. Concerted efforts to engage more actively with alternative fertilizer
businesses, such as early-stage ventures in biological products or larger-scale
projects in green ammonia production, conventional manufacturing and blend
ing facilities, are equally necessary to build the diversified supply base that
agrifood systems need. 5.3
INCREASE ACCESS TO AND AFFORDABILITY OF FERTILIZERS
A range of options could be used to improve farmers’ access to fertilizers and
address the constraints identified. Indirect approaches include investments in
infrastructure and a competitive transport market that reduces delivery costs,
resulting in lower farm-gate fertilizer prices. Governments may consider smart fertilizer subsidies combined with
other incentives as a policy option for increasing farmers’ access to fertilizers
and other soil nutrients. However, the impact of such subsidies is highly condi
tional on soil health, market access, weather reliability, and credit availability. Many of these conditions may be absent for the most resource-constrained
farmers, and previous programmes have fallen short because they were not in
place (Hill and Resnick, 2025). Redesigned smart subsidy models can improve
the efficiency of fertilizer use and restore soil fertility – provided they combine
support for bio-based and mineral fertilizers with incentives to invest in comple
mentary practices. Indeed, they may prove more sustainable than price support
programmes alone. However, in remote areas where infrastructure and market
access are major constraints, subsidizing fertilizer may be the least efficient use
of public funds. Where conditions are more favourable, targeted subsidies could
serve as investments facilitating access to complementary products and prac
tices that enhance nutrient use efficiency and restore soil fertility (Vanlauwe et
al., 2023). A further consideration is whether a portion of current subsidy spend
ing could be repurposed toward investments that generate higher and more
durable development benefits. For repurposing to be politically viable, alterna
tive investments should share the features that make subsidies attractive –
immediacy of benefits, visibility, and the ability to target specific beneficiaries.

Sequencing matters: the withdrawal of existing subsidies and the scaling of
alternatives must be carefully coordinated, with continuous monitoring of im
pacts used to refine targeting, assess soil and climatic conditions, and ensure
budget efficiency (Hill and Resnick, 2025). Improving producer access to credit can also facilitate access to fer
tilizer, as shown in the West African cotton systems characterized by interlinked
credit, input and output markets (Tsakok and Guedegbe, 2019; Tefft, 2010). Another policy instrument is developing inventory credit, which enhances pro
duction and fertilizer use by alleviating liquidity constraints at the onset of the
planting season, the critical period for access to inputs. 5.4
INCREASE PRODUCERS’ PRODUCTION INCENTIVES
The fourth objective consists of improving the incentives needed for producers
to invest in fertilizer and other productivity- and sustainability-enhancing meas
ures. A broad empirical literature confirms that smallholder farmers in SSA face
multiple, reinforcing constraints – insecure land tenure, lack of access to credit,
lack of appropriate research and extension, insufficient transportation and
market infrastructure, limited ability to manage risk, increased vulnerability
to climate change, weak collective action before markets and public power/
institutions, and a lack of access to complementary forms of income (Lowder,
Bhalla and Davis, 2025; Stewart et al., 2017). Critically, these constraints tend to
reinforce one another rather than operate independently, so that relaxing a sin
gle constraint in isolation may often yield limited results (Vanlauwe et al., 2010). POLICY AND INVESTMENT OPTIONS

For example, fertilizer subsidies introduced without improvements in output markets tend to have modest and short-lived effects. Extension efforts
unaccompanied by access to affordable inputs may change awareness without
changing behaviour. Soil restoration practices requiring upfront labour or
delayed returns are rarely adopted without income buffers or risk-mitigation
mechanisms. Effective production incentive policies therefore need to be
designed as coordinated packages, not sequential single-constraint fixes (Hill
and Resnick, 2025). Remunerative farm-gate prices represent a cornerstone of an im
proved incentive environment. Long-term price support programmes, if main
tained and consistently funded, can provide producers with the investment
signals needed to intensify production sustainably. However, price support
programmes often have a less-than-ideal track record and may pose an institu
tional risk of budgetary unsustainability due to substantial financial outlays,
particularly for public procurement and storage. Historical experience has also
shown that governments often lack the necessary resources to sustain mini
mum prices, especially in the face of significant downward pressure on those
prices. Governments may also need to enhance the provision of essential
public goods. Priority investments include rural infrastructure – particularly
roads and storage facilities – that reduce transportation costs and connect
farmers to markets. Harmonization of regional and sub-regional fertilizer regu
lations, including quality assurance processes, norms and standards, and
cross-border trade facilitation, represent additional public measures to make
fertilizer more accessible and more economically viable for African farmers. Crop insurance represents another option for de-risking farmers’
production environment and encouraging investment and use of productive
inputs. To date, liquidity constraints before planting, as well as diverse technical
factors, have restricted the adoption of crop insurance in sub-Saharan Africa. Subsidizing insurance premiums could make it more accessible to all farmers,
or to focus on the most vulnerable, significantly increasing uptake. Beyond price support and producer insurance programmes already
mentioned, a set of complementary investments has shown particular promise
in generating immediate, tangible, scalable benefits. These include digital advi
sory services, which provide timely, personalized guidance to producers, and
have been demonstrated to increase farmers’ profits in Nigeria. Additionally,
payments for ecosystem services can incentivize farmers to adopt environmen
tally friendly practices, such as shown in Ethiopia. Likewise, support to smallscale irrigation investments that reduce risks and enhance resilience may be
equally advantageous investments (Hill and Resnick, 2025). Each of these may
be effective in its own right, and may also address the underlying constraints
that limit fertilizer response, meaning they can make broader soil health invest
ments more productive, rather than substituting for them (Hill and Resnick,
2025). 5.5
CROSSCUTTING ISSUES FOR POLICY ACTION
In addition to the four policy objectives outlined in the previous sub-section, five
cross-cutting issues demand attention: (i) an enabling environment; (ii) innova
tive extension and farmer knowledge systems; (iii) investment in research and
development; (iv) enhanced de-risking instruments for farmers from financial
institutions; and (v) robust monitoring and evaluation systems, accountability
mechanisms and long-term, multi-sector planning frameworks.

Also deserving of attention is the need to address the issue of land tenure secu
rity. First, establishing an enabling environment and regulatory framework is
crucial for advancing sustainable soil health, fertility and fertilizer use in SSA. This requires strategic investment across all policy instruments to create con
ditions in which the private sector can thrive. Key tools include publicprivate partnerships that align private sector goals with national soil health pri
orities, supported by incentive-based policies that encourage both public and
private investment. Regulatory frameworks should be designed to promote both
the availability and responsible use of bio-based and mineral fertilizers across
the continent. Engaging farmers and private sector stakeholders in policy
dialogue and design can accelerate the adoption of sustainable practices such
as agroecological intensification.23 This approach, when supported by effective
policy tools, can deliver economic, social, and environmental benefits through
improved nutrient management, crop productivity and nutrient use efficiency in
SSA (Vanlauwe et al., 2023). 23Agroecological intensification prioritizes on-farm biodiversity conservation and nat
ural regeneration while reducing emphasis on soil tillage and chemical inputs. This
approach has evolved from a collection of isolated techniques into a comprehensive,
principle-based food production system. It strategically integrates conventional and
indigenous farming knowledge with agroecological science, implementing practices such
as cover cropping, agroforestry, green manure application, and minimal tillage. (Giller et al., 2021). Sustainable intensification has been defined as simultaneously
raising productivity, increasing resource use efficiency, and reducing negative envi
ronmental impacts of agriculture (FAO, 2026b; Vanlauwe et al., 2023). POLICY AND INVESTMENT OPTIONS

Second, revitalizing extension systems with consistent funding and testing
innovative knowledge systems can enable farmers to adopt ISFM practices,
including site-specific, customized recommendations, helping to catalyse the
sustainable intensification of African agriculture. Strengthening advisory servic
es can build farmers' capacity to innovate and develop ISFM approaches
grounded in agroecological principles and recommended mineral fertilizer ap
plication rates. Implementing improved practices requires substantial training
for technical staff to serve as facilitators, promote context-specific innovations,
and mobilize scientific and local knowledge. These advisory services can be
provided by the public sector, the private sector, NGOs, or farmers' organiza
tions, through traditional extension, farmers’ field schools, digital platforms, or
other innovative approaches. Capacity development is often necessary regard
less of the delivery model chosen. The Global Soil Doctors Programme in Africa
is one example of a successful farmer-to-farmer training initiative that has
demonstrated results in building farmer capacity for sustainable soil manage
ment (FAO and GSP, n.d.a).

Third, investment in research and development (R&D) at national and regional
levels is another cross-cutting strategy for enhancing soil fertility and fertilizer
use. To be effective, R&D efforts must be supported by comprehensive agricul
tural innovation systems that strengthen both research institutions and advisory
services. Long-term planning is essential to set priorities in soil health, fertilizers,
and agroecology research and innovation, as well as allocate human and finan
cial resources accordingly. Policymakers should implement effective incentive
structures to encourage private sector investment in agricultural innovation. This is key to creating a more robust and sustainable agricultural research eco
system (Fuglie et al., 2019), and integrating agroecological approaches into
production systems. While agroecology offers long-term advantages, its wide
spread uptake by farmers, particularly those using traditional methods, is a
gradual process that can be accelerated through targeted R&D and knowledge
dissemination. Fourth, financial institutions, including public development banks, are
well positioned to mobilize investment for improving soil health and fertilizer
use. They can do so by investing in large-scale soil testing facilities and ensuring
that site-specific recommendations can be made across the widest possible
range of territories, agronomic systems and farm households. Development
finance institutions (DFIs) could offer provision of first-loss capital and the draw
on African regional guarantee funds – such as the African Guarantee and
Economic Cooperation Fund (FAGACE), the African Solidarity Fund (FSA), and
the African Guarantee Fund (AGF). This strategic financial support helps to
mitigate the high production risks associated with agriculture. Fifth, robust monitoring, evaluation and accountability mechanisms
are critical to ensuring the success of soil health and fertilizer initiatives. Continuous monitoring and learning from both past and current experiences
enables verification that policy and programme objectives are being met. Effective oversight also serves as a safeguard, helping to prevent trade distor
tions and minimize opportunities for corruption. This function is best supported
by long-term, multi-sector planning frameworks that incorporate national fore
sight processes – systematic assessments of future trends, risks and opportu
nities – to guide resource allocation and priority-setting over time. Based on the issues presented in this report and the discussion of

Conclusion
This report emphasizes the importance of improved soil fertility and soil health,
increased fertilizer use, and greater fertilizer efficiency – grounded in “good
agricultural practices” – as foundations for sustainable agrifood systems in
sub-Saharan Africa. Historically slower productivity growth across the continent
reflects broader agricultural challenges, in which inadequate fertilizer applica
tion and poor soil health are both causes and consequences of imperfect
agrifood systems. While governments and regional groupings across the conti
nent are collectively committed to improving food security through higher
agricultural productivity, this report highlights the complex and multifaceted
challenges that stand in the way. Overcoming these challenges requires more
than just political commitment – it requires a coherent set of policies addressing
the diverse factors affecting fertilizer use, soil health and fertility, both within and
beyond the agricultural sector, backed by substantial investments that translate
commitments into action. Soil fertility functions as a conditional constraint: its importance for
productivity growth is undeniable, but the degree to which it limits productivity
varies considerably among farmers and contexts. Subsistence smallholders,
who dominate SSA's agricultural landscape, cannot ease soil fertility bottlenecks
without coordinated responses that simultaneously address risk, market incen
tives, land tenure, and infrastructure, alongside agronomic considerations. This
does not reflect a failure of technology, but the presence of multiple, reinforcing
constraints that shape farmers’ decisions. The implication for policy design
is direct: interventions that address only one constraint at a time – whether
fertilizer access, extension, or soil restoration – will consistently underperform.

Increased application of mineral fertilizer remains necessary across much of
sub-Saharan Africa to raise yields in the near term, complemented by proven
and financially viable agroecological and ISFM principles that build soil organic
matter and nutrient availability over time. The need is clear in sub-humid and
semi-arid parts of the continent and more fertilizers are also clearly needed in
rainfed production systems. The case for greater fertilizer use is reinforced by
evidence that fertilizers are on average more productive in SSA than elsewhere.24
This is a consequence, in part, of the severity of soil degradation across the
region, which makes investment in soil fertility and health more urgent and more
impactful than in less degraded agrifood systems. Sustainable approaches
tailored to specific soil characteristics and farmer circumstances are especially
important in the most degraded areas, where blanket fertilizer application is
least likely to generate durable returns. This report argues that SSA countries do not face a binary choice
between mineral fertilizer-led intensification and exclusively bio-based ap
proaches. Most would likely benefit from a combination of complementary
policy instruments supporting both. Central to any such framework is attention
to the agronomic conditions of the soil itself – the key element of production. This implies a radical rethinking of fertilizer support programmes, moving away
from blanket fertilizer subsidies toward more flexible, differentiated support. This approach needs to account for cropping systems dynamics, recognizing
that intercropping, crop rotation, and crop–livestock integration are core soil
fertility strategies for many smallholders, not a transitional step toward some
other system. Recommendations and support programmes should be differen
tiated by farm size, agroecology, and market integration, and accompanied by
investment in knowledge and behaviour change. Connecting production areas
to dynamic consumption centres is equally important, with market integration
not peripheral to soil health policy, but central to the profitability and sustaina
bility of investments in production. The policy instruments outlined in this report address potential tradeoffs between short-term needs and long-term objectives. Short-term measures
alone are insufficient to feed growing populations sustainably, while long-term

7.2.2
Green ammonia
Green ammonia is produced via electrolysis, using renewable electricity. The
hydrogen produced by electrolysis of water is then combined with nitrogen from
the air to create anhydrous ammonia, which is the same output as traditionally
produced via the Haber-Bosch process for mineral fertilizers. A key benefit is
that despite being energy-intensive, the production of green ammonia can be
carbon-neutral. While most green ammonia production remains at a pilot stage, devel
opments are accelerating.26 The International Energy Agency (IEA) estimates
that by 2030 nearly 8 megatonnes of near-zero-emissions ammonia production
could be operational worldwide (IEA, 2021). Production is still in its infancy in
sub-Saharan Africa, but the pipeline of planned projects is growing, with flagship
initiatives in South Africa and Kenya (Hive Energy, 2021; Ammonia Energy
Association, 2022). Constraints for deployment include, first and foremost, the high capi
tal costs of large-scale production and storage infrastructure. Electricity
accounts for approximately 85 percent of the total cost of production (Royal
Society, 2020), making access to affordable renewable energy essential for
green ammonia development. A further constraint is that direct application of
anhydrous ammonia as a fertilizer requires specialized knowledge, and equip
ment beyond the reach of most smallholder farmers in sub-Saharan Africa. 26 This sub-section and the two that follow it draw on CASA (2023), which provides a clear
and up-to-date description of alternative fertilizer products and market
developments.

In practice, ammonia is most widely used as an intermediate product in the
manufacture of other fertilizers, and its direct use is confined to very few coun
tries – notably in North America – which account for 3–5 percent of global am
monia use. Inefficient application of the resulting fertilizers can have negative
environmental and health impacts, including water pollution and nitrous oxide
emissions. Moreover, the production process also has a significant water
requirement: electrolysis – the step producing the hydrogen used to make am
monia – requires large volumes of water. In short, while green ammonia offers the prospect of substantially
lower carbon emissions than conventional production, it faces considerable
technical, economic and environmental hurdles before it can become a viable
and sustainable fertilizer product (Santhappan et al., 2023). 7.2.3
Organic products
Organic products are material derived from organic compounds from animals
and plants that improve the physical, chemical and biological characteristics
of soils, provide nutrients and increase microbial activity (Bullor et al., 2024). Organic fertilizers include materials from livestock production operations used
for fertilization purposes, such as manure, urine, slurry, straw and other bedding
materials, (FAO, 2019). They also include compost (a mixture of decaying organic
matter, as from leaves, domestic waste and manure, used to improve soil struc
ture through the addition of carbon and provide nutrients), green manure (plants
that are grown in order to provide soil cover and to improve the physical, chem
ical, and biological characteristics of soil), crop residues (residues from previous
or other crops incorporated in the soil), mulch (plant material that is kept on the
soil or added to the soil for soil and water conservation purposes), marine waste
(organic fish amino acid and seaweed), biochar and bokashi. By and large, these
products support long-term soil health by increasing soil organic carbon,
improving soil structure and water holding capacity. They can also support
microbial activity, which in turn can support nutrient cycling, enhance resistance
against diseases and pests, and promote overall plant health and productivity
(CASA, 2023). The availability and uptake of organic products vary considerably
across and within sub-Saharan Africa, because of variations in farming practic
es, the level of access to organic materials, local knowledge and traditions,
policies, and farmer income levels. Organic products are often self-provided or
obtained in local informal markets, resulting in a lack of official statistics. In most
remote farming communities, organic “waste” is a misleading word as these
resources compete with other uses and can be in short supply compared to
demand. Organic fertilizers play a critical role in ISFM and in improving all soil
characteristics (physical, chemical and biological) and ultimately improve and
sustain soil health. For that critical reason, they need to be promoted and
strengthened by enhancing research and development to improve their quality
and accelerate their production in Africa as reflected in the Africa Fertilizer and
Soil Health Action Plan and the Nairobi Declaration (African Union, 2024b;
African Union, 2024d). For smallholder farmers in sub-Saharan Africa a blend of organic and
mineral fertilizers – where available – may offer an optimal benefit/cost ratio
in the future. A meta-analysis conducted in 2020 showed that combining

high-quality organic products with mineral fertilizers enhanced agronomic effi
ciency (the increase in yield per unit of nutrient applied) by 20 percent and
reduced SOC losses by 18 percent across seven cropping seasons, compared

and application costs per tonne, let alone the negative climate footprint of trans
port emissions. In addition, it can take several years to reap tangible benefits in
terms of soil health, which can lead to losses for farmers in the short term. In terms of sustainability, inefficient use carries some of the same risks
as mineral fertilizers, including nutrient runoff (albeit to a lesser extent given
lower nutrient concentrations), soil contamination (metal compounds, phtha
lates among other). The production and use of animal manure emits methane,
which is a powerful greenhouse gas. Depending on the product and context, the
impact of organic fertilizers can stimulate either nitrification (generally favoura
ble as it converts nitrogen to a form that can be more readily assimilated by
plants, potentially enhancing nitrogen use efficiency), or, inversely, denitrifica
tion (harmful under certain conditions, leading to increased production of
nitrous oxide). This can be difficult to predict in advance, making the blanket
prescription for “more” organic fertilizer products potentially counter-produc
tive and requiring a quality control framework. In any case, the use of mineral
fertilizers or organic fertilizers alone has some negative effects and ideally the
combination of organic and mineral fertilizers as a climate-smart ISFM practice
in sub-Saharan Africa has more beneficial effects. Results have shown that
combined application of mineral and organic fertilizers leads to greater respons
es in productivity and agronomic efficiency as compared to sole applications of
one of fertilizer types (Gram et al., 2020).

BOX 3
Local innovations in organic and organo-mineral fertilizers in SSA
Examples of emerging business models with the potential for scale at a local level
include well-organized production of organic fertilizers. These are produced in solid and liquid forms in various sub-Saharan coun
tries: Benin, Burkina Faso, Nigeria, Senegal and Togo in West Africa; Eritrea, Ethiopia,
Kenya, Malawi, Rwanda, Uganda, and the United Republic of Tanzania in East Africa;
as well as in South Africa. Mbeya organo-mineral fertilizer, produced by farmers in Malawi, is an
example of a homemade organic fertilizer created from locally available raw materials
combined with a small amount of inorganic fertilizer (FAO, 2025b). Kenya is home to several initiatives, including waste-to-fertilizer and
waste-to-biochar processes (CASA, 2023). Eritrea has had success through a joint effort between the Ministry of
Agriculture and the Ministry of Marine Resources to produce solid and liquid organic
fertilizers, including bokashi fermented organic fertilizer, organic fish amino acid,
and seaweed liquid fertilizer (Ministry of Agriculture, 2023). Eritrea has moved to
establish regulations on quality standards for organic fertilizer exports as part of its
collaboration between the two ministries to promote the production of these prod
ucts (Ministry of Information, 2024). 7.2.4
Biological fertilizer products
Biofertilizers (FAO, 2019) are defined as products containing living or dormant
microorganisms such as bacteria, fungi, actinomycetes and algae, alone or in
combination, which on application help in fixing atmospheric nitrogen or solubi
lize/mobilize soil nutrients. They are living microorganisms that can improve soil
health and crop yields. Biological fertilizer products (also dubbed “biofertilizers”) are naturally
derived substances and living organisms that can help to optimize nutrient
uptake by soil and plants. They are used to supplement either mineral or organic
fertilizers, rather than as a standalone input, and they help to transform nutrients
present in the soil (or applied with organic or mineral fertilizer) into forms that
are easily absorbed by plants. The distinction is usually made between biofertilizers and biostimu
lants (including seaweed extracts and humic acids, which work to improve
fertilizer efficiency). Biofertilizers are typically delivered via seed treatment
(coating seeds before planting), soil treatment (mixing into the soil), or root dip
ping (for transplanted crops). The method that is chosen depends on the crop,
biofertilizer type, and field conditions. A scant but encouraging set of case study evidence, including from
sub-Saharan Africa, shows positive outcomes in terms of improved yields of up
to 30 percent versus untreated crops (Schutz et al., 2018). One of the constraints
for deployment lies in the timing, frequency, and method of application, which
are critical issues that should be tailored as far as possible to specific crop and
soil conditions. In addition, specific storage conditions – in some cases refriger
ation – are needed to preserve the efficacy of living products, which can be

difficult to ensure during “last-mile” distribution in parts of sub-Saharan Africa
and represent additional logistical costs depending on origin, packaging, and
shelf life among others, leading to a high cost for the farmers to incur. Further,
development of biofertilizers in the region would require development of poli
cies, regulations, and rules for quality control (Raimi, Roopnarain and Adeleke,
2021). The largest customer segment to date is large commercial farms in
Europe, the United States, and other developed economies, with smallholder
farmers in sub-Saharan Africa still only a nascent customer group (Raimi,
Roopnarain and Adeleke, 2021), with early-stage development of biofertilizers in
countries such as Côte d’Ivoire for cotton production. Currently, research on use of biofertilizers in several crops is ongoing
in Africa (AATF and IITA, 2013). These include for sorghum in Ethiopia, Kenya and
Zimbabwe; for cowpea in Cameroon; for groundnut and bambara groundnut in
Madagascar; for rice in Rwanda; and for unspecified work in Burkina Faso, Côte
d’Ivoire, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kenya, Rwanda and Senegal. The UNESCO Microbiological Resources Centre (MIRCEN) project at the
University of Nairobi, Kenya has, since 1981, developed a Rhizobium inoculant
known as BIOFIX, which is the main inoculant currently available on the local
market and therefore used by farmers. Under the right conditions, biological fertilizer products have the po
tential to reduce the need for mineral fertilizers (by increasing the efficiency of
the fertilizer or enriching the soil with nutrients available to plants), reducing the
associated emissions and soil and water pollution (Saffeullah et al., 2021). 7.2.5
Organo-mineral fertilizers
Organo-mineral fertilizers combine dried organic and mineral fertilizers to pro
vide balanced nutrients along with soil health improvements in a long-lasting,
easy-to transport and store form (IFA, 2024).

Agriculture is a cornerstone of sub-Saharan Africa's economy, yet
it falls short of meeting regional food security and nutrition needs. Low
productivity is widespread, particularly where soil quality and health
have been degraded. Fertilizers can play a key role in breaking this
cycle, but only where conditions support their effective use. This
report by the FAO Investment Centre, in partnership with Agrinatura
and the European Union, examines the structural, market and agro
nomic constraints to improving soil health, and assesses the tools and
options available to address them. It finds that raising yields will re
quire increased mineral fertilizer use, complemented by proven agroecological and soil health management approaches. The evidence
points away from uniform solutions and traditional approaches that
